source.authors: Dwi Ariyoga Gautama, Hendro Susanto, Mochammad Riyanto, Ronny I. Wahju, Michael Osmond, John H. Wang
source.title: Reducing sea turtle bycatch with net illumination in an Indonesian small-scale coastal gillnet fishery

corrected_record.method: paired field experiment in a commercial fishery: illuminated versus unlit control gillnets fished on the same nights; Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test
corrected_record.conditions: Wild green turtles caught as bycatch off Paloh, West Kalimantan, Indonesia, and released alive; April 2014 to June 2017. 70 pairs of control and illuminated nets (140 nets), fished the same night 1 to 2 km apart. Lights were constant (non-flashing) green LEDs, peak 500 nm, every 10 m on the floatline; light intensity not reported; whether net assignment or side was randomised is not stated. Green turtles: 14 in control nets and 6 in illuminated nets, Wilcoxon p = 0.039 (test statistic not reported). Other species in the same experiment had very small counts: olive ridley 7 vs 1 and hawksbill 3 vs 2 (all turtles 24 vs 9; multi-species reduction 61.4% per the abstract, 60.7% in the Discussion). Catch per unit effort of total catch and target species remained similar between treatments (total marketable catch p = 0.370, target catch p = 0.096, non-target catch p = 0.655). Nets were set in late afternoon and soaked overnight (mean 12.4 h control, 12.1 h illuminated), 203 mm stretched mesh, about 1.2 km long; onboard observers recorded catch. Mean green turtle CPUE was 0.18 +/- 0.05 SE in control nets and 0.07 +/- 0.03 in illuminated nets (Table 3 prints 0.7, apparently a typo). The experiment compares nets, not animals: an effect of the lights on turtles is inferred by the authors, and the study cannot separate visual avoidance from other responses to the lit net.
corrected_record.quote: Results indicated that net illumination significantly reduced multi-species sea turtle bycatch by 61.4% and specifically green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas) by 59.5%, while the CPUE of total catch and target species remained similar.

source.authors: Dacyn Holinda, Joanna M. Burgar, A. Cole Burton
source.title: Effects of scent lure on camera trap detections vary across mammalian predator and prey species

corrected_record.method: field experiment: paired lured and unlured camera-trap stations, detection counts modelled with zero-inflated negative binomial GLMMs
corrected_record.conditions: Free-ranging mammals in Alberta, Canada, February to August in 2015 and 2016. 844 camera stations (404 lured, 440 unlured) at 247 sites, four Reconyx PC900 cameras per site about 600 m apart at the corners of a square, the cameras in the northeast and southwest corners lured with one tablespoon of O'Gorman's Long Distance Call (a skunk and musk blend) in a PVC tube staked 5 m in front of the camera and those in the northwest and southeast corners without (fixed corners, not randomised; the paper does not say whether unlured stations had an empty tube or stake, so a visual novel-object cue is not excluded, and does not state lure replenishment); data truncated to 120 days after deployment; events defined with a 30 min threshold to reduce the influence of animals investigating the lure; mammals were detected at 800 of 844 stations, with 7110 detections at lured and 7530 at unlured stations. Zero-inflated negative binomial mixed models with site as random effect; the authors assumed any lure effect lasted the full 120 days and removed zero-inflation from the wolf model. Per-species lured and unlured counts are not reported in the text read. Lure is a commercial product, not a defined compound. Same paper: predators as a group, large and small carnivores and fisher were detected more at lured stations; prey, small mammals and ungulates were not. Fisher: beta = 2.23 +/- 0.36 SE, z = 6.18, p < 0.001. Gray wolf: beta = -0.01 +/- 0.34 SE, z = -0.03, p = 0.973; Richardson's ground squirrel: beta = 0.00 +/- 1.14 SE, z = 0.00, p = 0.998; moose: beta = 0.07 +/- 0.15, z = 0.50, p = 0.621. The authors say the scent likely draws investigative predators into the detection area and can alter their movement, so detection is a detectability and movement outcome, not abundance.
corrected_record.quote: Scent lure significantly increased detections of predators as a group, including large and small carnivore sub-groups and fisher specifically, but not of gray wolf.
